statement.p: Let S be the cube with side length 2, faces parallel to the coordinate planes, and centered at the origin.
(a) Calculate the total flux of the constant vector field \vec v = \,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k} out of S by computing the flux through each face separately.
flux through the face at x=1:
flux through the face at y=1:
flux through the face at z=1:
flux through the face at x=-1:
flux through the face at y=-1:
flux through the face at z=-1:
Calculate the flux out of S for any constant vector field \vec v=a\vec i + b\vec j + c\vec k.

p.em: (Be sure that you can explain why your answers to parts (a) and (b) make sense.)

static.solution:
(a) For a flat surface, flux through \vec{A} is \vec{v} \cdot \vec{A}. Therefore, the flux through each face of the cube is equal to (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (\vec{A} \mbox{ of the face}).
First we shall find the flux through the two faces parallel to the yz plane, beginning with the one with positive x. A unit vector normal to this plane pointing outward is \vec i. Therefore \vec{A}= 4\vec i. The flux then equals (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (4\vec i) = 4. For the face with negative x, the unit normal vector pointing outward is -\vec i. Therefore \vec{A} = -4\vec i. The flux then equals (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (-4\vec i) = -4.
Next, we will find the flux through the two faces parallel to the xz-plane, beginning with the one with positive y. A unit vector normal to this face pointing outward is \vec j. Therefore \vec{A} = 4\vec j. The flux then equals (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (4\vec j) = -16. For the face with negative y, the unit normal vector pointing outward is -\vec j. Therefore \vec{A} = -4\vec j. The flux then equals (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (-4\vec j) = 16.
Finally, we will find the flux through the two faces parallel to the xy-plane, beginning with the one with positive z. The unit vector normal to this face and pointing outward is \vec k. The area of the face equals 4, so \vec{A} = 4\vec k. The flux through the face with positive z equals (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (4\vec k) = 4. For the face with negative z, the unit normal vector that points outward is -\vec k. Therefore \vec{A} = -4\vec k. The flux through this face is given by (\,\mathit{\vec i}-4\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}) \cdot (-4)\vec k = -4.
Adding up all of these fluxes to get the flux out of the entire cube, we get \hbox{Total flux} = (4)+(-4)+(-16)+(16)+ (4)+(-4) = 0.
(b) For any constant vector field \vec{v} = a\vec i + b\vec j + c\vec k, we can calculate the flux out of the cube by the same method.
Let's find flux out of the two faces parallel to the xy plane, beginning with the one with negative z. A unit vector normal to this plane, that points negative (because of the orientation of the face) is -\vec k. The area of the face equals 4, therefore \vec{A} = -4\vec k\). The flux through \vec{A} then equals (a\vec i + b\vec j + c\vec k) \cdot (-4\vec k) = 0+0-4 c = -4 c. For the face with positive z, the unit normal vector pointing outward is \vec k and we similarly get a flux through the face of (a\vec i + b\vec j + c\vec k) \cdot (4\vec k) = 0+0+4 c = 4 c.
The calculation for the other faces proceeds similarly, and we see that the contribution through each pair of opposite faces will cancel, so that the total flux will be zero.
The answers in parts (a) and (b) make sense because the vector field is constant, and so it does not change as it comes in the one side of the cube, and exits the other side. Therefore the two fluxes cancel each other out, making the total flux zero.
